title: Accelerating Dense LLMs via L0-regularized Mixture-of-Experts
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 18 Sep 2026]
    Title:Accelerating Dense LLMs via L0-regularized Mixture-of-Experts
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance but suffer from slow and costly inference. Existing acceleration methods often lead to noticeable performance degradation, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models require extensive computational resources. In this paper, we propose L0-MoE, a lightweight MoE approach using L0-regularization to accelerate dense LLMs nearly without performance loss. Our method introduces a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation and applies dynamic batching for efficient training. Experiments show that L0-MoE achieves up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines.

report.summary: L0-MoE converts dense LLMs into sparse mixture-of-experts models using L0 regularization, achieving up to 2.5x inference speedup with minimal performance loss.
report.background: Large language models deliver strong quality but are expensive to run because dense architectures activate all parameters for every token. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce inference cost by routing each token to a small subset of experts, but training MoE from scratch is resource-heavy and can suffer routing instability, load imbalance, and domain mismatch. Existing acceleration techniques such as quantization, pruning, distillation, and speculative decoding often trade quality for speed. L0-MoE enters this context by retrofitting dense LLMs into sparse MoE models using L0 regularization, aiming to retain dense-model accuracy while gaining conditional-compute efficiency. The paper also targets practical training bottlenecks with domain-aware data curation and dynamic batching, reflecting the industry's broader push toward cheaper, faster inference without retraining giant models from scratch.
key_points: The core idea is to add L0 regularization to a dense LLM so the model learns to activate only a small set of experts per token. This converts a dense network into a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model, cutting computation during inference while preserving most of the original model's behavior.

The authors introduce a cluster confusion matrix for domain-aware dataset curation. By measuring where the model confuses different domains, they can assemble training data that encourages experts to specialize meaningfully, rather than creating redundant or poorly routed experts that waste capacity.

Dynamic batching is used to handle variable expert loads during training. Because different tokens may route to different experts, naive batching creates padding and underutilization; dynamic batching improves hardware efficiency and makes the MoE conversion process more practical on standard GPU clusters.

Experiments report up to 2.5x speedup over dense models while maintaining competitive performance, outperforming existing LLM acceleration baselines. The claim is notable because many acceleration methods lose noticeable quality; L0-MoE aims for near-lossless acceleration via sparsity rather than aggressive compression.

The approach suggests a path to upgrade existing dense checkpoints without full MoE pretraining. If reproduced, it could let teams add sparse inference to models already in production, reducing serving costs while keeping the same base weights and fine-tuning recipes.
report.impact: For the AI industry, L0-MoE reinforces the shift toward conditional computation as a primary lever for lowering inference costs. If the 2.5x speedup holds broadly, cloud providers and model labs could serve larger models at lower cost, intensifying competition around efficient architectures and MoE serving infrastructure. Developers may gain a way to convert existing dense checkpoints into sparse models, but they will also need expertise in routing, L0 regularization, and MoE deployment, plus careful validation to avoid hidden quality regressions. Regular users could see faster responses, cheaper API pricing, and more capable models available at the same budget. Caveats remain: results are from one paper, and real-world gains depend on hardware, batch size, task domain, and whether expert routing generalizes outside curated data.
report.tools: Follow the paper's code release, if any. Relevant tools: Hugging Face Transformers and PEFT for model editing; DeepSpeed-MoE, Megatron-LM, and Fairseq for MoE training; vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM for MoE inference; Megablocks for sparse expert kernels. Also watch open MoE models such as Mixtral, DeepSeek-MoE, Qwen-MoE, and OpenMoE to compare routing and serving approaches.
